prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how reallocation across firms shapes exporting, foreign investment and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B019 with Kiyotaki and Moore, and I said I was not settled on the order of B019 and B010. After the exchange I now prefer B010 with Melitz and Helpman. The reason is the evidence record and the credit line, not the number of members who prefer it. My own work is about testing contracting theory on real contracts, so I look for a mechanism that makes sharp predictions and has met data repeatedly. Melitz (2003) does this. It generates predictions on who exports, exporter premia, entry and exit, and within-industry reallocation after liberalisation, and these have been checked on firm-level data in many countries over more than twenty years. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus FDI adds a second, separately tested prediction about how firms organise across borders. That gives a two-name credit that follows the intellectual structure of the contribution. B019 is a conceptually foundational single mechanism, and I still hold that view. But in round 1 I conceded that its direct empirical identification is weaker than the theory's influence suggests, and that the 2022 adjacency and the accelerator strand leave a boundary that members could not settle. Friberg, Hjalmarsson, Dreber and Enflo made the evidential point, and Boppart and Teorell made the boundary point. Both points hold weight with me. The distinctness question from the 2008 prize is answerable on substance: representative-firm new trade theory does not produce selection into exporting or aggregate gains from reallocation across firms. On the chair's wording question, I would draft the citation around firm heterogeneity, selection and reallocation, and say nothing of Helpman's broader career. The scientific background would then acknowledge the Bernard-Jensen exporter facts, Eaton-Kortum and Hopenhayn as precursors or parallel strands. The citation could not claim all of modern trade for the two laureates.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real. Redding, Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum and Hopenhayn have claims outside the pair, and wording and the background document only partly repair that. The size of the gains from selection depends on parametric assumptions such as Pareto productivity draws, so the qualitative mechanism is better established than the welfare magnitudes. The citation should therefore not reward a particular number. The Committee must also be satisfied that the contribution is distinct from the 2008 trade prize. I think it is, but that is a judgment the Committee should test explicitly. On the other side, B019 gives up some mechanism-level elegance when set aside: a single collateral-feedback loop with two clear originators and about thirty years of use in macro-finance and crisis analysis. If the Committee decides the 2022 theme is not saturated and weights conceptual foundations over breadth of confirming evidence, B019 is the stronger case. My own field proximity may make me over-value contracting-based mechanisms such as B019, which is one reason I discount that tilt here. My assessments rest on my own recollection of the literature and I have not independently verified them.

responses.point: Boppart keeps B019 first with Kiyotaki and Moore. He treats B010 as a serious alternative, but argues that B019 has tighter single-mechanism attribution and that B010 has real precursor-credit disputes with Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum. He also says Gertler as a third name would be natural but is better left out because of the 2022 overlap with Bernanke.
responses.response: I agree with your two-name boundary for B019. That is why I dropped Gertler in round 1 and why I do not defend a three-name B019 now. Where I now differ is how to weigh the two cases. Clean attribution on B019 comes with an indirect evidential record and an unresolved boundary to the 2022 prize. B010 has a larger precursor question but a narrower and better-tested core. Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extension are the identifiable origin of selection and reallocation, and the omitted strands (exporter facts, Eaton-Kortum) can be named in the background without changing who is credited. I treat that as a smaller citation risk than the one B019 faces. Our difference is about weighting a single clean mechanism against confirmation, not about whether B019 is foundational. I would keep B019 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B010 first and flags that Eaton-Kortum and Bernard-Jensen sit outside the credited names. He wants the citation kept to the firm-heterogeneity discovery without a lifetime-achievement framing for Helpman. He also asks whether Redding belongs in the core.
responses.response: I agree on the citation scope and have drafted mine to match: firm heterogeneity, selection, reallocation, and the exporting-versus-FDI margin. I would keep Redding out of the core. His main contribution is quantitative and spatial trade, built on this framework, and a third name would turn a clean origin credit into a later-extension credit. On the precursors, I would not widen the laureate set. The Bernard-Jensen facts motivated the model and Eaton-Kortum is a parallel quantitative route, so both belong in the scientific background. I would add one caution to your framing. The citation should not imply that the welfare magnitudes are settled, because those depend on distributional assumptions. This is a point on which we seem to agree.

responses.point: Teorell moved from B019 first to B010 first. He says the credit boundary for B019 (Gertler, Gilchrist, Bernanke) is harder to settle than for B010, and that field balance should not decide among candidates on scientific merit.
responses.response: I agree with both points, and your path is close to mine. I accept that Kiyotaki and Moore are the cleanest B019 core and that the accelerator question cannot be settled by the Committee quickly. I also agree that field balance after 2008, 2022, 2023 and 2024 should not override the common criteria of significance, attribution and maturity. I would add that the thematic adjacency of B019 to 2022 is a significance question and not only a balance question. It bears on how large the marginal conceptual advance is. I do not think that adjacency disqualifies B019. It does lower my confidence in the B019 citation compared with B010, where the credit question is narrower.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B032 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She argues that the China-shock evidence on local labour-market adjustment is scrutinised and credible, and that continued debate over magnitudes shows testing, not fragility. She narrowed her set to avoid overlap with Goldin's 2023 prize.
responses.response: I accept your point about debate being evidence of scrutiny, and I keep B032 as my second alternative because the transparent, well-identified design appeals to me. Two things keep me from preferring it. The entry bundles two strands, the trade-shock empirics and the task framework, and the task framework has antecedents outside the ballot (Acemoglu, Restrepo, Levy, Murnane). Your narrowing to the trade-shock core is a sensible response, but it makes the award an empirical programme on one episode. The long-run aggregate picture is also unsettled. B010 offers a general mechanism with the same kind of data-based confirmation and a shorter credit list. I still think your wording, which claims reshaped labour demand and local adjustment and no settled welfare conclusion, is the right way to draft a B032 citation.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee judges the heterogeneous-firm contribution distinct enough from the 2008 trade prize, and whether the Bernard-Jensen, Eaton-Kortum and Hopenhayn credit can be handled in the scientific background without a laureate-set change.
How far the qualitative selection and reallocation results survive productivity distributions other than Pareto, and whether the welfare magnitudes should be left out of the citation entirely.
Whether Redding is better treated as a later quantitative and spatial extension or as a co-core contributor; I treat him as the former but weigh this as a judgment, not a settled fact.
Whether my move away from B019 underweights its conceptual foundations and the post-2008 relevance of collateral-based amplification, and whether the 2022 prize really leaves room for it.
My assessments rely on my own recollection of the literature and on colleagues' statements, not on independently verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: Updated: my preferred part is now B010 (Helpman, Melitz), and no co-authorship, institutional tie or other personal connection to either name is apparent from my supplied profile. Under B019, my earlier disclosure stands: I am a corporate-finance specialist and John Moore's incomplete-contracting work is intellectually adjacent to my financial-contracting research. That ties it to my first alternative and not to my preferred part. I hold an adjunct appointment at Chicago Booth and an SSE professorship, and I am a Vice President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. No candidate affiliation is recorded in my profile. These are disclosed and not adjudicated.
